render.title: How ATP slows glycolysis by inhibiting phosphofructokinase
render.body:
Phosphofructokinase-1 (PFK-1) is the main control point of glycolysis. It catalyses the conversion of fructose-6-phosphate to fructose-1,6-bisphosphate — a committed, irreversible step. Because this reaction cannot easily be reversed, controlling PFK-1 is an efficient way for the cell to regulate the whole pathway.

When the cell already has plenty of ATP, it needs less glucose to be broken down. ATP itself acts as an allosteric inhibitor of PFK-1. It binds to a regulatory site on the enzyme (distinct from the active site where the reaction happens). This binding changes the shape of PFK-1 in a way that reduces its activity — the enzyme becomes less effective at catalysing the reaction, so glycolysis slows down.

The cell also uses the ratio of AMP to ATP as a signal of energy status:
- High ATP (low AMP): PFK-1 is inhibited and glycolysis slows.
- Low ATP (high AMP): AMP activates PFK-1 and glycolysis speeds up.

Citrate (an intermediate of the Krebs cycle) provides a second inhibitory signal. When the Krebs cycle is running well and citrate accumulates in the cytoplasm, it also inhibits PFK-1, signalling that the cell does not need more acetyl-CoA from glycolysis.

This allosteric control is fast and reversible: when ATP levels drop, the inhibition is released and glycolysis resumes. The overall effect is that the rate of glycolysis matches the energy demand of the cell — a neat example of feedback regulation.
render.summary: PFK-1 is the key regulatory enzyme of glycolysis. High ATP allosterically inhibits PFK-1 by binding a regulatory site and reducing enzyme activity. High AMP has the opposite effect. Citrate provides a second inhibitory signal. Together these controls match the rate of glucose breakdown to the cell's energy needs.
